utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start the cross-examination of the next witness, I'd like to raise one procedural issue, although only briefly. The Chamber has received the response by the Defence on the new, I would say, series of 92 bis witnesses. In many instances, the Defence thinks it is not necessary to call that witness for cross-examination if certain redactions are ordered by the Chamber, or at least if it's taken out. Has there been any communication between the parties to see whether they could agree on -- so that the Chamber could focus on those redactions where the parties would not be able to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't seen that yet, but based on prior experiences with the Defence, I think we oftentimes have been able to agree to redactions. I'm not sure precisely which ones you're referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the new series. So that's not the Prijedor, but I think it was filed the 29th of November. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. The response was due on the 29th of November. It was filed on the 29th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So the Prosecution should have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, I think that Mr. Gaynor, of course, has quite some carriage of the 92 bis issues for the Prosecution. I don't know if he's in a position to clarify matters any further. But in any event, what Mr. Hannis has indicated to the Court is correct. We have not had any discussions in relation to those redactions since we filed the Defence response in relation to that second series of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll take a look at the first break, Your Honour, and see if we have, and if not, we'll track it down, and we'll try to give you a response right away. But based on our past experiences we've often been able to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice very often it's lines referring to an opinion of the witness or if it's a rather general statement where the witness does not clarify what the source of his information is, and sometimes it even might not hurt that much for the Prosecution to the extent that there may be other elements of evidence that would perhaps cover and sometimes in more factual terms the issue at stake.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would very much like to hear from the parties whether there's any agreement on that by next Wednesday, if that would be possible. Then Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour, but I had a short conversation with Mr. Gaynor prior to coming into court this morning, and there's a question of a slight amendment to the indictment that the Prosecution seeks to make. It's just in relation to moving a particular mosque from one municipality to another, as it were, in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that both parties agree that the municipality in which the Ahatovici mosque is supposed to be located is not a correct one and it should be in Novi Grad rather than in -- I've forgotten which one it is. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I think it was Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was not Vogosca, I think but another municipality. The parties both agree that whether or not proven, but it makes no sense to situate that mosque anywhere else than in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. That seems to make complete sense and the Defence has, of course, no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it it is an oral application to amend an annex to the indictment to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I can read out the details now for the record if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Question. If you would please do so, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, schedule D to the indictment, the mosque listed as mosque 17.5, which states: "Mosque at Ahatovici" is erroneously listed under the indictment of Nevesinje. It should be listed under the municipality of Nevesinje. It should be listed as being within the municipality of Novi Grad. We don't suggest any massive renumbering of the indictment. What we suggest is that Novi Grad be inserted as municipality 17B and that the mosque at Ahatovici could be referred to as 17.B.1, and we would seek leave to amend the indictment in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, you told us already that you would agree. You also agree with the technicality of the solution, renumbering -- giving Novi Grad the number 17B for the mosque and identify the mosque under 17.B.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence has no objection to that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request is granted, Mr. Gaynor. Now I suggest that you at least make that list perhaps only that page if you could fit it in new so that we get a new copy. At least one of the whole list, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Would you like us to file with the Registry an amended page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you amend that page and if it fits on one page, and if the pages are numbered, I don't have that in my mind, but at least the items are numbered, then I think that that would be sufficient. Everyone is now warned not to use old versions of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if there's no other procedural issue to be discussed at this moment, I'd like to ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Mujkic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mujkic. I do not receive any translation. Is the -- because I heard you say good day, but ... Are the microphones, are they on? Could you perhaps come a bit closer to the microphone, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, it's really quite some time ago that you were here and that you gave testimony, that you were examined in chief. Since such a long period of time has passed by, I'd like you to renew your solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and may I invite you, Madam Usher, to hand out the text of the solemn declaration to Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. Please be seated. Mr. Mujkic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas, counsel for the Defence. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, good afternoon. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I think that you've given a total of three statements to the -- in relation to these matters, and I'll just take you through them. The first one was in 1996, to the Bosnian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, to the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the second one was to the Tribunal in 1997?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This was just a newer version of the earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think you gave a further short statement in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in the offices of the Tribunal at Nedzarici, in Sarajevo, two times.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Two times. Now, and I think just before coming here to give evidence on the 3rd of November, you also supplied the Prosecution with some additional information on the 1st of November, 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because it was here at the Tribunal that I was given some telephone intercepts, wherein my name was mentioned, and I merely gave some remarks by way of an addition.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you gave -- you stayed in the offices of the Tribunal at Nedzarici in Sarajevo two times. Do you recall the dates of those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Loukas. I wasn't really interested in the dates, because at the time I did not really know that I was going to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, on the last occasion when you gave evidence, on the 3rd of November, you gave some evidence in relation to the position of Mr. Krajisnik's house. You recall that, of course?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I take it you're aware that Mr. Krajisnik was not living in that house in the period April to December 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, and I cannot testify to that. As for the time in question, at that particular time, I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course, Mr. Mujkic, not from April to December, not the entire period, of course. You're not saying that, are you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April there were already barricades in place, and one could not cross the bridge at Reljevo. It was in late March that the first barricades or checkpoints were placed, put up for the Muslims. And there was no need for me to go down there, because we would go to Sarajevo, across the bridge at Bojnik, near Butmir. That was the main communication link with the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But in any event, it's not correct to say that you were in prison for the entire period of April through December of 1992, is it, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in prison between 6 August and 25 October.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to another aspect of the evidence you gave on the last occasion. You'll recall that you gave evidence in relation to speaking to certain of your neighbours in relation to the killing of a number of people in what has been described as the bus incident. Do you recall the aspect of the evidence that I'm talking about here?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention the bus, because I wasn't present there. I only said that from the stories of the survivors, because there were eight survivors of the bus massacre. All of them had identical stories to tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Mujkic. That's the aspect of your evidence that we're talking about. Now, these people you indicated in your evidence are your neighbours; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And they're people that you know well?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Can you give the Court the names of these eight people?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm going to remember them all. Do you want me to take the order of their age, from the eldest to the youngest, or vice versa? Anyway, the bus incident was survived by the following villagers: Asim Gacanovic, Dzemal Mujkic, a relative of mine; Emir Mujkic, a relative of mine. Novalija Osman. He was my peer. We went to school together. Elvir Jahic. He was here. You know him. Muhamed Usto. He was the only one that remained unchafed, wasn't hurt at all at the bus. Dzemal, another person who survived the bus incident but whose family name I cannot recall. He went to Austria and lives there to this day. I might have left someone out, but these were more or less the people who survived. And also Zaim Rizvanovic who was the fifth son -- there were five sons in that particular family, and he was the only one to survive. The other four died. Had I known you would have asked me this, I could have taken -- brought a list with me, because as secretary of my local commune, I was in charge and drafted myself the lists of all those who were killed, not only at the bus but in general. And you can find that at the Dobrosevici local commune, because I communicated with all the relatives to write down their fathers' mothers' names and ages. Among them were these eight survivors, and had I known, I would have brought these papers with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. That's quite adequate for my purposes. Now, just going to your statement from 1997, on another topic. You indicate there that: "On the 31st of May, I left Ahatovici. We had been informed that two platoons from Visoko had been sent to help us." Now, these two platoons from Visoko that you refer to in your statement, how many men were in these two platoons?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my relative who was killed in the bus, he sent me, he was the -- he was a member of the Crisis Staff, because I did not have any small children nor elderly at my home, and I had the weapons, and I was familiar with the area. And I was asked to join a unit belonging to a -- run by a member of the Crisis Staff. We were supposed to clash with two -- to actually meet up, link up with two platoons who had -- who were coming to help us, and we wanted to go ahead and meet them in order for us to avoid friendly fire. However, this other man, Novalija, I was unable to find him because he got under fire from the Serb forces, who attacked Bioca and started heading towards Ahatovici. So I actually came across the Serb army, but there were bushes there and luckily I could hide from them. I noticed that these were not Meho and his group. I never saw them again. As for the two platoons, it is true, and I heard a story later on from those who were members of the platoons, they did head up and heard shelling halfway and actually returned. So I cannot tell you how many there were in these platoons, because in actual effect they never showed up, although they set out initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, you finally came to the answer to the question. It took you approximately three minutes to get there. If you say "I don't know the size" and if Ms. Loukas is interested to know why you could not know the size, she'll certainly ask you. So perhaps begin with the core of the question when answering. You always can add something if needed. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And do you know the --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know how many men there were, because the men never showed up. And I never met up with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- it's now clear to us. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, you're aware, of course, from your giving evidence on the last occasion that we are of course subject to time limitations, and I just want to echo what His Honour has said. If you can answer a question with a "yes," then please do so. If you can with a "no," please do so. If you want to explain a little further, the importance is that you actually answer the specific question that I'm asking. Because I have some questions to ask you, and we don't want it to be that you stay here longer in The Hague than you need to. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and we will go along that way. But your question had to do Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond with how many men there were, and I had to tell you that I did not know their numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, what was the ethnicity of the men in these platoons?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what sort of a question is this? I never met these people, because I stayed in the woods, because I came across the Serb forces, and the following day I went back to Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, you do understand that the Judges have to decide this case. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you don't take offence at me asking you questions, do you? I take it that's a no.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because you understand that the Judges need to hear your answers to questions from both the Prosecution and the Defence; you agree with the way that the system works, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I mean, and you also understand that neither you nor I are going to decide this case. That's for the Judges. You appreciate that fact; yes?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that it's only fair, in terms of justice, that both sides --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, Ms. Loukas, please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honour, I mean, I want to avoid the sort of problem that we had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not see that the answers until now create any necessity to ask a fourth question in this direction. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to leave it at three, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, the platoons that you were going to meet, you had some awareness that the men in the platoons were predominantly of Muslim ethnicity; you were aware of that, were you not, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that, because I was not a member of the Crisis Staff and did not have any information as to who was going to Hum. I was just told that these were two platoons. But one can assume that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you referred to a relative of yours being a member of the Crisis Staff. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Hasan Mujkic was, of course, the commander of a paramilitary formation in Ahatovici, or I take it you disagree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree because the Territorial Defence, of course now depending on one's perspective, had the purpose for the people to defend their own houses. It did not have the equipment and materiel that an army disposed of. It simply meant that every family would dig up trenches in front of their houses, in front of their homes, to defend themselves. Now, whether you can speak of the TO in military terms, I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Mujkic was the commander. But what I meant to say was that I don't know why that would be a paramilitary unit, when the person is actually simply defending one's own home.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes that the earlier answer also had a paramilitary, not a military, mentioned by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Loukas, you are a bit confusing the witness, I take it, because where you said so your answer is no, your question was whether he disagreed with that proposition. If the answer would be no, then it would mean that he did agree, but that's not what I had in mind you put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's the negative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'll recall that you gave certain evidence on the last occasion in relation to Mr. Mirko Krajisnik. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mirko Krajisnik -- or rather, there was this third delegation, if one could say so, that arrived on the 6th of August, 1992, past midnight, and that was the commander of the Rajlovac Brigade, Apostolski, who I had known as an active-duty-officer, a captain, and he introduced me, the archduke Nikola Poplasen, who demanded that I tell him who was present there at Ahatovici, and since my jaw was broken, I was unable to speak and he told them, Well, give him a piece of paper. He is literate. He can write down. And Mirko Krajisnik was with him. There was another man who had a very -- he was very well-groomed, had a beard, but he was not introduced to me, and I don't know him, whereas Mirko Krajisnik I had known from before, and there was no need for him to be introduced to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Right. So you're saying that Nikola Poplasen was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and as was said, the archduke, "nadvojvoda."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And who is the archduke?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vlasto Apostolski, the commander of the Rajlovac Brigade military police, told me that he was the archduke. Later on, he was also the president of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that Apostolski was there and Poplasen was there, and Mirko Krajisnik was there; is that correct? Is that a correct summary of what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another person, a man who had a very neat beard. He was not introduced to me, so I could not tell you who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to take you back to some evidence you gave on the previous occasion. Now, before we go to that, so you're certain of that, that these are the four people that were there; correct? Apostolski, Poplasen, Mirko Krajisnik, and a man with a neat beard; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just take you back to something you said on the last occasion you gave evidence here, on the 3rd of November, 2004?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we request page numbers when reference is made to previous--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certain. Page 80 of the transcript of Wednesday, the 3rd of November, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have the transcript of the day and not the numbering going through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's exactly right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, well, let's be -- we all know how to count, isn't it? If you would know what the first page of the day is, Mr. Gaynor, you add 80, you arrive at the right page. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just getting back to what we were talking about, that was, of course, the 7th of August, 1992 that we were talking about, the early hours of the morning; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, Ms. Loukas is asking you whether it's correct that you're talking about what happened in the course of the morning of the 7th of August, 1992. Mr. Mujkic, I take it that you cannot confirm that that's on page 80 -- you have that in your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought she was addressing you. That's why I kept quiet and did not respond. Yes, these were the early morning hours of the 7th of August. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll take you back to a question and answer on the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond last occasion. I hope Mr. Gaynor has found the relevant portion of the transcript. Now, you were asked this question: "I'd like to take you now a few hours after that incident, the early morning of the 7th of August, 1992. Is it right that you were visited by a number of men?" That was the question asked of you by the Prosecutor on the last occasion you gave evidence. And this was your response: "Yes, that was my third visit, the third visit to my cell that night. It was towards morning, towards dawn on the 7th of August. Major Vlasto Apostolski came in. He was the commander of the military police of the Rajlovac Brigade. And three men came in after him. He introduced them and said first: This is nadvojvoda, or super-leader, and the other two were Mirko Krajisnik, who I recognised. I didn't recognise the third man and he didn't introduce him either." And then your evidence goes on in relation to the conversation that occurred, and you were asked this question on the following page by the Prosecutor: "Do you know the name Nikola Poplasen?" And your response was: "Not until that time, but the man was the president of the Serbian Republic and President Petric replaced him." The next question was this: "Did you see Nikola Poplasen at any time in August 1992?" And your answer was: "I didn't see anybody, just the people who came to my cell. So no." Now, you recall those questions and answers that were asked of you by the Prosecutor on the last occasion?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, today you tell the Court that Nikola Poplasen was there. You agree with that; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, he was introduced to me by Vlasto Apostolski. He said: "This is Archduke Poplasen."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it the Prosecution concede that he denied that Mr. Poplasen was there on the last occasion. So I can shorten this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree that in the -- that the transcript reads as was reflected by Ms. Loukas. I'm not sure that there's any concession involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the Prosecution agrees on the text, not necessarily on your interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the interpretation is clear. I would have expected a concession from the Prosecution on that point. I take it there's no concession forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear any such thing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mujkic, you said on the last occasion that, that's on the 3rd of November, that you didn't see Nikola Poplasen, but today you tell the Court that you did see Nikola Poplasen; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I ever saw that he wasn't there then. I may have said I hadn't known him before. I saw him even later on television. But I don't recall saying that I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's have a look at your statement in relation to this matter, from 1997, page 5, for the benefit of the Prosecution. In your statement, when dealing with your being visited in the cell - this is the statement taken in 1997 for the Tribunal - you said that: "When I was in Rajlovac," and I quote, "I was visited by Goran Lemez and a Major Vlasto Apostolski on the 7th of August, 1992. I asked Goran for a cigarette. The Major told me his name is not Goran. He is a duke. Goran had a lot of paper regarding other prisoners." So in 1997, the people you have visiting your cell on the morning of the 7th of August, 1992 are Major Vlasto Apostolski and Goran Lemez?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was around 10.00 a.m. on the 7th. Goran Lemez was a neighbour of mine. He was the duke of that part of Ahatovici, which was a surprise to me, because we had been very close before. We had been good neighbours. I asked him to bum a cigarette. He refused. And Vlasto Apostolski told me: "He's not Goran. He's a duke. That's the way you should address him." And I hadn't known that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look at your statement from 1996 that you gave the Bosnian authorities. You there refer to again the 7th of August, 1992. This is at page 9 for the benefit of the Prosecution. You say that Mile Tintor came in to see you, with Vlasto Apostolski. So that's another person.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was already the afternoon, the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mujkic, you don't mention Mirko Krajisnik in your statement in 1996, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this submission came about, or why, but my point in telling all this was to show how we were treated by people who were our neighbours until the day before. And I concentrated on Mile Tintor and the other one, what's his name? Thanks to Tintor, I wasn't beaten again in my cell, because he had ordered Vlasto Apostolski to stop the beatings. My jaw was broken by that time and I couldn't speak. And nobody, indeed, took me out for beatings any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, no one's arguing that you have suffered a lot. This is not what this is about. This is about the fact that you mention Mr. Krajisnik's brother, Mirko Krajisnik, in your evidence on the 3rd of November, and you don't mention him in your 1996 or 1997 statement, and you concede that, of course; yes?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to add one thing here to give you a more realistic, broader picture. I hadn't known anything about the stories concerning my exchange, because nobody contacted me directly. I was only allowed to speak when given permission or when asked something. But when I was shown those intercepts, where Bakir Alispahic and Mirko Krajisnik were discussing me, then the memory came back that he had visited me in my cell to make certain -- to make sure that it was me. And in the telephone intercept, he says: "Yes, I know the man." The first time I gave a statement, I hadn't been aware of that. In fact, I didn't know about that until I came to The Hague. And at the time, it didn't seem important or relevant, in 1996. If I had known the whole story, I would have mentioned it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, when you gave evidence today, you said that Nikola Poplasen visited you in your cell, and you don't say anything about him visiting you in your cell in 1996 or 1997 either, Mr. Mujkic, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention Nikola Poplasen or Mirko Krajisnik or the third gentleman, because at that time it was just a meaningless visit to me. It was here for the first time that I realised that it was important for my exchange and that he had come to make sure that I was indeed the person he was interested in. Because the stakes were rising. Fifteen sniper shooters were required in exchange for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, I want to take you back to your supplying the additional information to the Prosecution on the 31st of October and the 1st of November, 2004, just prior to giving your evidence on the 3rd of November. What you told the Prosecution then was that Nikola Poplasen, Mirko Krajisnik, and a bearded man came to question you in the military police building in Rajlovac, in the early hours of the 7th of August, 1992. You agree with that, correct, that that was what you told the Prosecution the weekend before you gave evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Then, when you come to give evidence, you leave out Nikola Poplasen, on the 3rd of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't really understood you. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, when you gave evidence before this Court on your solemn declaration, you said that you hadn't seen Mr. Poplasen that morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, because why wouldn't I mention it here if I saw him?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. When you were specifically asked the question, I'll quote Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond it directly to you: "Did you see Nikola Poplasen at any time in August 1992?" Your answer was: "I didn't see anybody; just the people who came to my cell. So no." So we're agreed that when you gave evidence on the 3rd of November, you said that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe -- you took the whole month of August to deal with -- maybe I skipped it accidentally, but on the 7th of August, he did come into my cell. He was introduced to me by Vlasto Apostolski. Otherwise, I hadn't -- I wouldn't have known who he was. His surname is very unusual, and I don't know anyone else with the same surname in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, being fair, 12 years after the event, are you prepared to concede that you could be wrong about seeing Mirko Krajisnik in your cell in the early hours of the morning, 7th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not wrong, because with Mirko Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik, and with their father, in early spring 1992, I sat at the same table.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. 1991.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the funeral of their relative, Vlado Gogic. I was 44 years old at the time. I was not wet behind the ears. And I'm not wrong, because I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So what was the date of this funeral that you sat next to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was early spring, maybe late March or early April. I cannot tell you the date because it wasn't important to me. The relative had been killed in a car accident. He lived near the Butile barracks, and I saw him every day and was on nodding terms with him for years. So I came to the funeral of this Vlado Gogic. He took my arm and he said: "You belong at our table." I cannot be wrong, because only a year later, the same man came into my cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, my question was the date of this funeral, Mr. Mujkic. So if you could please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you: Early spring. And I cannot tell you the date because it had nothing to do with the war. It was 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but the answer is very long and it doesn't -- you did answer my question, but it took you a long time to get there and we have a lot of material to get through, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, but you can't blame the witness for not answering your question, because that's the first two lines of his answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he said: "It was early spring, maybe late March of early April. I cannot tell you the date because it was not important to me." That's what --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: . I'm talking about the previous answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is -- this is -- the date is 1991. This is the funeral that you say you sat next to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, let me take you back to the information you gave the Prosecution on the weekend before you gave evidence in relation to this matter. What you said there was that you sat next to Momcilo Krajisnik at a funeral in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what you told the Prosecution on the weekend of the 31st of October and the 1st of November, 2004, just before you gave evidence a month ago.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the year was recorded that way here, because I corrected the paper two or three times, and it was sent back for retyping. I don't know how this mistake found its way into my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you say that the Prosecution made a mistake; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the proofing - and the Prosecutor is here, he can confirm - I returned this statement two or three times for retyping because of interpretation errors. I don't know how come this error remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Gaynor would care to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be happy to clarify one small point here. Mr. Mujkic is talking about the intercept sheet of analysis which he was shown several times, which he corrected and then signed. That's what he's been referring to right now. Ms. Loukas, on the other hand, is referring to the supplemental information sheet which the witness did not have an opportunity to correct, that was drafted by me on the basis of answers received during the proofing session and then disclosed to the Defence and to Your Honours. So there is a slight misunderstanding in relation to what he was shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I take it that Mr. Gaynor's not saying that he put the piece of paper together, the supplemental information sheet, incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No. As I said, the supplemental information sheet reflects what the witness told me. But he did not himself correct it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, you've heard what the Prosecutor has had to say in relation to this. Are you prepared to concede that it's possible that you've made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When, Ms. Loukas? Giving his statement, giving his testimony? And apart from that, the possibility to make a mistake is, I would say, a general statement. Could you please be specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, are you prepared to concede the possibility that you've made a mistake in giving your evidence today in relation to saying it was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was indeed in 1991. The error is 1987. I don't understand how this error was made, because it's pretty far away from the truth. I told you: I knew the man very well. He lived three houses further down the road from the barracks. I saw him literally every day for years. I don't know how I could be so badly mistaken. It couldn't be 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, you, of course, listened in court to the intercept of a conversation between Mirko Krajisnik and Bakir Alispahic on the last occasion you gave evidence. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course, in that intercept, you will recall Mr. Mirko Krajisnik does not say anything about actually seeing you, does he?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not mention seeing me, but he said: "I know him," which means that he had seen me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So when you were shown the intercept between Mr. Mirko Krajisnik and Mr. Bakir Alispahic, was that what prompted you to make the mistake of saying in court that you'd actually seen him on that morning, the 7th of August, 1992, something you'd never mentioned in any previous statement that you'd signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to object to that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few matters mixed up in your question, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to break it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to break it up, but I think the general sense of what I'm putting to the witness is there and it contains its various aspects. But I'm more than happy to break it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, you were shown the intercept between Mr. Mirko Krajisnik and Mr. Bakir Alispahic, and that intercept, as you know, was dated the 20th of August, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date of the intercept, whether it was the 20th or some other date, but I did listen to it here, and it was this intercept that triggered the memory of his visit to my cell. Because in his conversation with Bakir Alispahic, he says: "I know." However, the warden of the prison, Vlaco Brane, brought me a paper and said: "You can be exchanged this evening, tomorrow, or never. Five people from the other side in exchange for you. Of course, if they are unharmed." I at that moment had no idea who was negotiating what. All I could see was that piece of paper. And then when I heard the intercept, I realised what the role was of Bakir Alispahic and how the stakes were rising in my exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And your evidence is the Prosecution showing you the intercept triggered your memory of seeing Mr. Mirko Krajisnik there; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, I would have never mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, I'm just going to show you the transcript of the intercept between Mr. Mirko Krajisnik and Mr. Bakir Alispahic, which is P381A.1, exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the original will be shown to the witness, that is, P381A, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, have you got that intercept before you, Mr. Mujkic? Can you please have a read of that intercept --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- and tell the Court where in that intercept Mr. Mirko Krajisnik says that he knows you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that can be a basis for the inference that he knows me. He says: "He is badly injured." So he means -- that means he knows me, and I think there is another reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So that's what you're relying on for the indication that Mr. Mirko Krajisnik knows you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is -- yes. And Bakir says at one point: "You know, his father had only one leg." And the answer is: "Yes." There is no reason for me to lie about the two of us knowing each other. Perhaps somebody else minds, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, let's move on to another topic. On the last occasion you gave evidence, you indicated that when you were at Planjo's house, -- before we go on to that, just a second. Just in relation to that last answer, where you say: "Bakir says at one point, you know, his father had only one leg, and the answer is yes." Right? Can you tell me what page that's on, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't managed to find it here now, because of the shortage of time. I don't know whether it's contained in this particular intercept or some other. But let's take a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, it might help if you go to the page number that has 03288029 at the top of the page. Right at the bottom of that page, there is: "What can you do to pull that man out? He will lose --"

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- that he also lost his leg. Mirko Krajisnik doesn't say he knows. He says: "We agreed on some kind of exchange for him."

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it here now. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So why were you telling the Court that that was in the transcript when it wasn't, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have sworn to have heard him in this intercept saying: "I know."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mujkic, let's move on to another topic. The last occasion you gave evidence, you were giving evidence in relation to what happened at Planjo's house. For the benefit of the Prosecution, the transcript reference is page 91. You give some evidence there in relation to people being forced to eat cigarettes and a matter -- a sexual matter connected with that. And also, people being told to jump from a first floor and being asked to jump onto concrete. Do you recall that evidence you gave on the last occasion, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll remember it as long as I live, and that's true, but it wasn't concrete down there; it was gravel.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you will agree with me, Mr. Mujkic, that you did not mention any of these matters in your 1996 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you something. My statement given to the police in 1996 was actually a result of them asking me vaguely: Where were you? Nobody was putting specific questions to me. When I came to Sarajevo from Zenica in 1995, there was this high-ranking officer there and I was supposed to clear out my status. And he told me: Well, you were living with the Chetniks for four months there. And it nearly turned out as if I had been supporting the Chetniks. And then I started talking and then they said: "Okay. Why don't you give us a statement." And there I did not mention all the events, the Planjina house and other troubles that I went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But of course when the Prosecution interviewed you in 1997, the next statement you gave, of course they did ask you questions, did they not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1997. We were simply sifting through my 1996 statement and practically it did not change much.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course your 1997 statement was very detailed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We were going into some detail because the gentleman from the OTP then told me that there was a possibility for me to go to The Hague to testify and whether I was willing or whether I had any apprehension in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course, before you signed it, they asked you if you had anything to add; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall now. I didn't see the statement again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I take it you're saying that these serious matters that you left out of your 1997 statement with the Prosecutors is because they weren't asking you the right questions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we must object to that. This is another example of wrapping up things that the witness clearly hasn't said. It's a summary based on evidence which the witness hasn't given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, whether the right questions or the wrong questions are asked, the issue is whether he was asked about it. That's what the witness says. You're introducing a few matters that do not reflect the testimony of the witness. But of course you can seek confirmation on whether it was because he was not asked about those matters that he did not say anything about it. And you could ask him whether he considered those matters to be serious matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So let's just go back to that, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I was just checking a matter on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: When the Prosecutors were taking your 1997 statement, of course, they did ask you to tell them everything you knew, did they not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked to say anything. It was the gentleman who was putting questions to me, he just simply had in his hands this 1996 statement that I gave to the Bosnian police, and he said: "Well, would you want to read the statement perhaps?" I said: "There's no need for that. I know what I went through." And then he put some questions to me that were not really in any sort of an order, like the questions you're putting to me now, and I was simply answering him from my knowledge. Because this is something that I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll show you a copy of your statement. Mr. Mujkic, if you could turn to the last page. Would you like to read out to the Court what it says there under "witness acknowledgment"?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This statement has been read over to me out loud in the Bosnian language and it is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991, and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So are you saying that's not true, that you signed something that wasn't true there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, fine. If this is the original. Because I don't see my signature here. I don't see it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I can show you the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you're putting to the witness that he has not stated to the truth. Do you mean that while not everything is in there, that that's the reason why it's not true, or is it ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he indicated that he gave his statement and he -- let me see the precise wording there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "It's true for the best of my knowledge and recollection."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In relation to his answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry. In relation to his answer at page 30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I don't want to go any further with the witness with his headphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, could I ask you to take off your headphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour will see that answer the answer at page 30. The question I asked is: "When the Prosecution were taking your 1997 statement, of course, they did ask you to tell them everything you knew, did they not?" His answer was: "I was not asked to say anything. It was the gentleman who was putting questions to me. He just simply had in his hands this 1996 statement that I gave to the Bosnian police and he said, Well, would you want to read the statement perhaps? I said, There's no need for that. I know what I went through. And then he put some questions to me that were not really in any sort of an order, like the questions you're putting to me now. And I was simply answering him from my knowledge, because this is something that I lived."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still do not understand what the basis is for your -- did you not tell the truth. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's indicated that the statement was not read out to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, the original statement, the statement he gave to the -- to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, well, Your Honour, the 1997 statement. Because my question was related to the 1997 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's still not completely clear to me. But if you perhaps ask specifically in what respect the statement might not have been true. Mr. Mujkic, could you please put on your earphones again. That's what you can't hear. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, just to go back to this question of the 1997 statement: Was it read out to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1997 or now?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your 1997 statement, was it read out to you when you finished giving it to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. Believe me, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, obviously you were asked if you wanted to add anything, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not have really added anything. That was the gist of it. Or rather, an outline of everything that had happened. Had I known that the situation was going to be as it is today, I would have written it down for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, in your 1997 statement, you don't mention these matters that you gave evidence of on the last occasion about what had occurred at the Planjo house. We're agreed on that, are we not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned it at the time. You see, the questions put to me were: How did this happen or that other thing, how did it happen? But other specific questions were never put to me, for the exchange, when I was in the hospital, I had nothing to eat there. I lost 33 kilos at the time. And there were other such matters that I never mentioned at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness has to be asked to speak at a decent pace. This is impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, the interpreters have some difficulties in following the speed of your speech. May I ask you to slow down. And Ms. Loukas, if you could find somewhere in the next two or three minutes, a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to -- I'm about to go on to another topic. I'm about to leave Planjo house behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break first, Mr. Mujkic, and we'll continue at a quarter past 4.00. Madam Usher, could I first ask you to escort Mr. Mujkic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, do you have any idea on how much time you'd still need for the remainder of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, there's not much left at this stage. We're in the home run, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this information. We'll then have a break until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the Chamber apologises for this late start, when the Chamber urged the parties not to come late. But it had good reasons. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Mujkic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, Ms. Loukas will resume her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, in late May 1992, you met a group of Albanian soldiers who suggested to you that you come into the army barracks with members of the TO while they were on guard duty, so that you could take over the army barracks in Butile?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the soldiers of Croat ethnicity were leaving the army, whereas those of Albanian ethnicity were unable to, because the Croat soldiers had their certificates testifying to the fact that they were students enrolled at a university, and there was this procedure that every six months you had to go and renew this booklet. Whereas those who were ethnic Albanians among the soldiers, they were mostly uneducated, illiterate and were unable to obtain such certificates. On one occasion, it was after the 20th of May, I was on my bicycle passing near the Butile barracks on my way to a friend of mine. There were those PAMs there, the anti-aircraft guns. And one of those in the barracks recognised me. They came -- they approached the wire fence and they told us: Mujkic -- they told me: "Mujkic, could you get us out of here? We've been here for a while." I responded to them that I was unable to help them because I was no longer able to enter the premises after the 9th of May. They told me, Well, that only drunken soldiers were standing guard there now at the time. But I knew that this was an impossible mission to fulfil for these people to be freed, and this never took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll just indicate, Your Honours, I'm informed by Ms. Cmeric that there's an omission in that -- the last sentence of the translation, whereby it should include: But I knew that this -- right. That these Albanian soldiers could take over the barracks was an impossible mission. So there's just that small bit missing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was the impossible mission being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I highly appreciate this, especially also the assistance of Ms. Cmeric in not losing any part of the transcript. Originally spoken words. At the same time, Ms. Loukas, I have to stress that it's not just a matter of correcting the translation. It's always a matter of finding out whether. So therefore, the best way is to, if something seems to be missing, to ask the witness whether he remembers exactly what he said and then invite him to repeat it that so that we get the missing part included in it, rather than to say: What was missing? Because then of course you could listen at the audiotape again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but I'm trying to avoid that situation, because I think Ms. Cmeric is rather overloaded with listening to audiotapes and making corrections on transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But you could resolve that then and say Ms. Cmeric draws my attention to the fact that there might be a part missing. And then you ask the witness to repeat that part of his answer, and I take it he'll repeat that in a complete sense, and we have the missing part there instead of already telling us what is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But I'm happy for the witness, if he remembers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need at this moment. I don't think that there's a -- it's of such relevance that -- although you never know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to this question of taking over the army barracks in Butile, Mr. Mujkic. The situation is that you informed Mr. Hasan Mujkic about this; correct? This proposal from the Albanian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the Crisis Staff, that is, to Hasan Mujkic's house, where the Crisis Staff was based, and I conveyed to them this information. However, this was cynical, because I was a member of the communist league, and this was almost a precondition for a person working for the JNA. So I was for them a Commie, a communist, and as I was working at the JNA barracks, he told me: Well, we were TO. We had no units to take control over anything. The orders were not to move anywhere but just to stay put and defend our homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last sentence, Mr. Mujkic, because the interpreters could not grab it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As concerns Hasan Mujkic and the Crisis Staff, for them, I was a communist, because I was a member of the League of Communists and worked for the JNA for 24 years. And he cynically told me: You Commies, what are you doing here? What do you want here? We have no units to go around conquering anything. We can only defend our own homes. And this was simply out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In fact, I think Mr. Mujkic, when you told him about this plan, said to you that he operated exclusively by the order of Mr. Alija Delimustafic, did he not, the minister of the interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that. He added that, that they had the orders. Alija Delimustafic was a person that I report to, and there were no orders to go around taking control of anything, but merely to stay put and defend our homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in fact, three or four days after that, a message did come from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Crisis Staff and I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What, you're not aware that three or four days later, a message came from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I was a communist to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mujkic, is it possible you've said something like that before, that Mr. -- that a message came three or four days later from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a story that went around the village. I personally was not involved in any of it. I wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff. I merely heard the story talked about by the women concerning what the Crisis Staff was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So who did you hear that from, that a message had arrived from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just telling you now: These were women spreading these stories. I was not any sort of a military observer, nor did I receive any information from anyone that would make me informed. I merely heard these rumours, and I did not hear anything about the attack or any of the orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Didn't Mr. Mujkic actually show you a fax from Mr. Delimustafic saying that the army barracks in Butile should not be attacked?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a fax in his office, and when I said what I said, namely, that I was given a call by soldiers of Albanian ethnicity, he sent a fax to Delimustafic immediately, and shortly afterwards, he received the answer: Don't touch the barracks. And I saw that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And three or four days later a message came from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over. Didn't you hear that from -- is it possible that you also heard that from Mr. Hasan Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I never went again to the Crisis Staff, because that same evening, they told me: "You Commie have no place, no business being here."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll show you, Mr. Mujkic, a copy of your 1996 statement in B/C/S. Do you see the portion there on that page that relates to -- at page 4 in the B/C/S version, in about the middle of the page, do you see the portion that I am referring to there: "I informed the commander of the TO, Hasan Mujkic, about this, but he told me that he exclusively operated by the order of Alija Delimustafic, minister of the interior, at that time, and he showed me a fax message that he had received which said that the army barracks in Butile should not be attacked. Three or four days later, a message came from Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over. It was already too late because we found out in the meantime the intervention units of the Serbian volunteers called White Eagles had arrived there." Do you see that portion of your statement there, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in this first paragraph, where it reads that he showed me the fax, that was on the occasion when I told them about those Albanian soldiers, and he never showed me the second fax and I never said he did. It was just a rumour making the rounds around the village, and nobody showed me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'd agree with me, Mr. Mujkic, that you don't say anything there about that order from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over was just a rumour being put about by women?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say so here, but that's the truth, because I didn't see the second fax and the statement doesn't say that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've gotten that last sentence there it was already too late because we found out in the meantime. Who was the "we"?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. Now, on the last occasion you were here, Mr. Mujkic, giving evidence on the 3rd of November, you indicated there that, in relation to this question of arming, you indicated - and this is page 8, for the Prosecution's benefit and the Trial Chamber - the villagers of Ahatovici were armed with hunting weapons. There were two hunting carbines. You also indicated there that they were people who were hunters and so they had carbines for hunting. And also 15 people went to Visoko at the end of April, and even at the beginning of May, perhaps, 12 people came, and they were exchanged at Pale from Bratunac and they stayed in Ahatovici. So they brought their weapons with them. Do you recall giving evidence to that effect on the last occasion you were here, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that this was discussed here at all, but it is true. Don't pin me down on it, on the number of people who left, but when they came back, there were 12 other people with them who had been exchanged at Pale and who had families in Sarajevo. Because this was the only way to reach Sarajevo. They reached the checkpoint at Bojnik bridge, which stopped them and didn't let them go on towards Sarajevo. So they stopped in Ahatovici and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were aware that people from your village were going to buy weapons and get supplies from the Territorial Defence in Visoko in about May, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something I heard from other people. I didn't know that, because I wasn't part of the Crisis Staff so as to know the details about who went where, who bought what or got whatever, by whichever means. This was just the talk of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I take it that you wouldn't be able to disagree, then, that some 85 weapons were brought, approximately 85 weapons were brought at around about that time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree because I didn't count them. I don't know how many weapons were brought in. Nobody ever gave me that information. Because I told you in their book I was a Commie and I was at the barracks until the 9th of May, so they didn't trust me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, it was the situation in your local area that checkpoints had been set up in your villages, in the villages of, in fact, Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, and in fact night patrols, in about April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no checkpoints in Ahatovici. That's an error. There were checkpoints only at the two bridges across the Bosna River, in Reljevo and in Bojnik. There were no other routes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You say there were no checkpoints in Ahatovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll show you your 1996 statement, Mr. Jukic -- Mr. Mujkic, sorry. It's open at page 3 there. It's towards the bottom of the page in B/C/S. Have you found the portion there where it says: "Armed Serbs set up barricades on the road as early as March, as an introduction into war activities, and they controlled the traffic and passages with a constant maltreatment. As a reply to their activities, we also set up checkpoints in the villages of Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, and night patrols subsequently complemented the day patrols." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is rather hard to read. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution wish to concede it's there or should I get Ms. Cmeric to read it out?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Ms. Loukas appears to have read it out correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, do you want to take back what you told the Court earlier, that there were no checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no checkpoints in Ahatovici. There was no passage, no other route available except through Ahatovici, and the part of the road between Dobrosevici and Ahatovici was free of checkpoints. A checkpoint means a roadblock and control over who is passing through. There was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Was there a headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company in your village, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Headquarters of the 3rd Platoon? I don't even know about any division into platoons, because I really wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff. I know nothing about such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of a meeting round about 12th of April, 1992, held in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who went to which meeting? Meeting between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It was a meeting with local municipal representatives of Ilidza, Vogosca, Rajlovac. That rings no bells for you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a Serbian meeting, then. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you are not in a position to confirm that at that meeting, Mr. Krajisnik said neither Muslims, Serbs, nor Croats will leave Bosnia? You have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about that. It's not in my statement and I cannot comment upon something I don't know. What is reflected in the statement is my own life. I didn't say anything else, and I can say nothing about places which I had never been to.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Mujkic. Now, were you aware of a meeting in the second half of April 1992 held in the cultural centre in Reljevo, which was attended by Serbs, Muslims, and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat: I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I was working at the barracks at the time. And some things were deliberately kept from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And were you aware of weapons being obtained in Zabrdje, both by Muslims and Serbs, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war. I hear it from you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Mujkic, that you were not aware of a plan by paramilitary soldiers from Ahatovici to link Sarajevo and Visoko via Rajlovac? A yes or no would be fine.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to explain first what you mean by "paramilitary."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You don't know the word "paramilitary"?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the word "paramilitary," but in relation to whom, to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That there were soldiers from Ahatovici that had a plan to link Sarajevo and Visoko via Rajlovac. Were you aware of a plan of that nature? That's what the question is directed to. And you can answer it with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How do you conclude that it was a paramilitary formation when people were defending their own houses? It seems that in your eyes the best man is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, initially the question is whether paramilitary soldiers were linking or at least whether there was a plan. Then since you explained to Ms. Loukas that you had some difficulties with the paramilitaries, then she reformulated her question, and then she asked whether there were soldiers from Ahatovici that had a plan to link Sarajevo. So forget about the paramilitaries and answer the question, please, whether there were soldiers who wanted to link Ahatovici to Visoko via Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours: I repeat. I was not part of the Crisis Staff. Things were being kept for me. And there were no formations, no units there capable of mounting any such activity. Because we didn't have a single machine-gun, not a single mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question whether you were -- was whether you were aware. I do understand from your answer that you were not aware and that whether it could have been the case is something you doubt, but you have no personal knowledge of that. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
