utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear from anybody about anything like that in that period. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to put additional questions to Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There will no re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might have some questions for the witness, but I'd first like to consult the parties on the issue that is on my mind. Mr. Mujkic, would you please take off your earphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to know from the parties, since we heard some evidence, which it's not quite clear to me, as a matter of fact, how relevant that is, about who visited Mr. Mujkic when he was in detention. It seems to appear from the transcript that a Nikola, who was the best man of Mr. Krajisnik, according to the interlocutors, visited Mr. Mujkic. That's one. It also seems from this conversation on the 20th of August that Mr. Mirko Krajisnik - and when I just said Mr. Krajisnik, I also refer to Mr. Mirko Krajisnik - that there seems to be a need to inform him about that visit of this Nikola. It's -- first of all, it's not entirely clear to me how important it is to the parties, because is this Nikola, in the view of the Defence, Mr. Poplasen, or I hope that I've pronounced his name correctly, of which I understood the first name is also Nikola, is that the understanding, that he might have visited, or is that -- I do not know who the best man of Mr. Mirko Krajisnik is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. That's clear. So that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, just in relation to this particular aspect, it's certainly the situation on which I would certainly be very interested in hearing from the Prosecution in what way they seek to use this sort of evidence. I mean, if they don't seek to do anything with it, one wonders, of course, why it's called. But if they call it, of course, then we have to deal with it. Your Honour, and I would say, in view of the fact that this information or this evidence in relation to Mirko Krajisnik comes some 12 years after the event is not mentioned in any previous statement, that Your Honours might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're commenting rather than --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But Your Honours might consider excluding it in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor, what's the position of the Prosecution? If Nikola is not the Nikola, as we heard testimony about before, then it's less surprising that if the witness correctly has testified - I do not know whether he did or not - but if he has correctly testified that if that Nikola Poplasen visited him together with Mirko Krajisnik, then it's less surprising that Mr. Krajisnik is not aware of that other Nikola to visit the witness. But it's not entirely clear to me what the position of the Prosecution is in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just confer with Mr. Hannis for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submission, it's clear from the witness's testimony that Mirko Krajisnik was at that meeting, and that's the core point. The presence of Nikola Poplasen at that meeting will -- the relevance of that is not yet critical to us, but it may become critical at a later stage in the trial, when more evidence concerning Poplasen may be admitted. But it's certainly a matter which if Your Honour wishes to explore further with the witness, we'd certainly welcome that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Ms. Loukas, you say, of course, it's not in evidence, but what's the position as far as the best man of Mr. Mirko Krajisnik is concerned, if it's not Nikola Poplasen? Is it something you could reveal to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I'm happy to reveal it. It's not a matter of, of course, of which -- it's the forefront of our minds when taking instructions, the best man. But in any event, Your Honour, Mr. Mirko Krajisnik's best man is an entire different Nikola, who now lives in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are you in a position to identify him further, apart from that he lives in the United States? There might be a few hundred thousand Nikolas left.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can indicate that we think the last name is Ateljevic. I hope my B/C/S pronunciation hasn't mangled the pronunciation, but I think that Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik probably has a better idea of the name of his best man rather than his brother's best man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand, but sometimes brothers know from each other who their best men were. But I do understand there were more of them, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And I will explain another culture nuance, Your Honour, that the term "best man" doesn't necessarily mean best man at a wedding, as we might understand the term in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this information. Then there's no need to ask any questions to the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please put his earphones on again. You told us that -- let me find the right term, Mr. Mujkic. You told us that there were no checkpoints in Ahatovici, and Ms. Loukas confronted you with a portion of your 1996 statement. Perhaps we could try to see what exactly you meant when you gave that statement. Perhaps I could, if I may, Ms. Cmeric, ask your cooperation again to read at page 3, and then the line where in English it reads: "Armed Serbs set up barricades." I take it that it starts after the word [B/C/S spoken]; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read that slowly, and could I specifically ask the attention from the interpreters for the technical terms used for whether these are checkpoints, barricades, control. Could you please read it slowly, Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] "As early as March, the armed Serbs have, as a prelude to the war activities, set up checkpoints on the roads and controlled traffic and passengers with regular mistreatments, harassment. In response to their actions, we also blocked the access roads to Ahatovici and Dobrosevici. Gradually, we complemented the night patrols with the daily ones." [In English] I believe that's the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the relevant portion. Mr. Mujkic, hearing again what your statement says in the -- in your own language, is this a correct statement? I notice, and I say this to the parties, that the translation is not exactly what it is in writing. For example, I draw your attention to that it's "access roads to" rather than "in." And apart from that -- but let me first ask the witness. You heard it in your own language. Could you tell us whether this is a correct reflection of your statement.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is accurate or not, but I can tell you for a fact that except for the two roads across the bridges of Reljevo and Bojnik that were held by the Serbs, there were no other checkpoints anywhere controlling the passage of people or vehicles. Because these two bridges were the bridges of the trunk roads leading to Sarajevo. Dobrosevici were a predominantly Serb village, and there was no way that any Muslims could have set up any checkpoints there, nor were there any such checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be shown his statement, the original page 3. Mr. Mujkic, may I invite you to not only to look at page 3, but also to look at page 4, where more of a signature appears. Is this a statement you signed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature cannot really be made out. The one on page 5 is a clear one. The one on page 4 is quite illegible. And the one on page 3 doesn't really seem to be a signature, at least not on this piece of paper I have before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it's cut off rather than --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see what I just read to you about the -- in response --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see one half of it, whereas the lower part ... Your Honours, if a checkpoint is set up, then there must be a round-the-clock crew of people manning it 24 hours a day. Whereas here it says we blocked the access roads to Ahatovici and Dobrosevici. There's no point really to block both the roads to Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, because Dobrosevici was a predominantly Serb village. Gradually, night patrols were complemented by the daily ones. These were just guard posts. There was no actual checkpoint as a barricade on the road, and I can guarantee that with my own life that nobody ever placed a checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was there, if there was no checkpoint? You explained to us what a checkpoint would need and ...

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roads were passable, but there were these observation posts some 20 metres or more on a hillock. It was on the point where the road was forking off, actually, to the three villages: Dobrosevici, Ahatovici, and another one. And there was just this observation point to observe who was using this road, but nobody was really being restricted in their movement, nor could they have been restricted. So there was no actual checkpoint. There were two checkpoints on those two bridges I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that in response to those checkpoints at the bridges, you were -- well, let's say your side also took some initiative to have a better control on who or what moved on the roads. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the sole purpose of it. There was no checkpoint, believe me. Because if one is unable to move, then one is unable to move. If you have water in a glass, then it can't go anywhere, and that was true for us. We were unable to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did these activities initially take place during the day and later on also during the night?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day the whole place was being observed, whereas in the evening we would stand guard. You had my house. That was next to a road. And behind the house, in the courtyard, we would just place two sacks of sand or something and then stand guard. And you were simply there to observe who was moving around, to defend one's own home. But this was no checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, the only thing I'm doing is asking for your comment on what seems to be your own statement. So, therefore, I hope you don't blame me for doing that, because I'm reading the text which is clearly part of at least a written statement on which your name appears and which you have not denied is your statement.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to illustrate this to you: The arming of the Serb population, for instance, there were no trucks with weapons using these main roads. They were using side roads because they knew that we were observing the area, not because there was anything blocking them from passing. And the purpose of the exercise was to see who was going where, what was going on. Because we wanted to see what it was that they were bringing in with the military trucks, because the Serbs, they had weapons, and of course they were using these side roads to bring in weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That clarifies your testimony to me. Is there any need to put further questions to the witness triggered by questions put by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, this, then, concludes your testimony in this Court. Unfortunately, you had to come twice to give your testimony. The Chamber appreciates that you took the effort to come two times, that you came this long way to The Hague two times, and we'd like to thank you for having answered all the questions of both Prosecution, Defence, and of the Bench. I thank you for coming and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, you may escort Mr. Mujkic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would just want the truth to come out, because, unfortunately, my people have suffered, and this would be the greatest of rewards for me to prove their innocence and to show that this was just senselessness ruling. I have my wounds that will never heal. I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is fully aware of the wounds it may have inflicted upon you, and this Chamber and the parties are seeking the truth. That is important, and that also demonstrates the importance of witnesses to come and to testify. Thank you very much. Madam Usher, you may escort Mr. Mujkic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, perhaps we first go through the exhibits, both those from the 3rd of November, and I don't think we have gone through them already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will now read the list of exhibits introduced through Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P371, pre-marked map and legend. P372, order by Rajlovac municipality Crisis Staff, dated 09/04/1992, and English translation. P373, press release dated 11/05/1992, and English translation. P374, bulletin of daily events, number 114, and English translation. P375, declaration of Ramiz Mujkic dated 01/11/2004. P376, Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of BiH, handwritten notes of conversation of 05 June 1992. And P376.1, English translation. P377, report Romanija Birac Security Services Centre Sarajevo, dated 03/06/1992, and translation. P378, ruling of the Vogosca Serb municipality dated 8 July 1992, and English translation. P379, photograph showing Planja's house. P380, list of the Serb municipality of Vogosca prison unit regarding persons detained in the prison on 3 September 1992, and English translation. P381, CD of intercept between Bakir Alispahic and Mirko Krajisnik. And P381A, transcript of P381, and English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since there seem to be no objections, all exhibits ranging from 371 up until 381 are admitted in evidence. I suggest to the parties, since we had a rather long list at the end of the testimony of Mr. Mandic, that the registrar will print out the relevant part of that list, that the parties can review it, see whether they agree with the description, see whether there's any objection, and we don't have to read it all in court, and then go through them all in more general terms. Since the exhibits are always identified when they are introduced, so therefore it might not be necessary to read them all out again. Then I have one other procedural issue, unless the parties would have one they'd like to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's just one matter in relation to the exhibits just admitted. I can indicate there for the sake of the record, there is a translation issue with one of the documents. But, of course, as usual, we can liaise with the Prosecution in relation to that question. But I just want to put that on the record so that we don't lose sight of that particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will hear from that if the parties cannot -- even if the parties can resolve the matters, then nevertheless we'd like to have the right translation in front of us. The procedural issue I would like to raise is the issue of adjudicated facts. The Prosecution was invited to reorganise its list of adjudicated facts, or its list of facts tendered to be admitted as adjudicated facts. I do understand that the -- we have now a list of 784 instead of 1147 facts on that list. I also do understand that from those 784, 100 facts are under appeal in the Kvocka case, and that from the remaining 684 facts, that 500 have already been admitted by the Chamber, whereas 184 now in the new reorganised list are pending. The Chamber invites the OTP to file the list as it is right now, so after it has been organised, but without the facts which are still under appeal in Kvocka. We might come back to them at a later stage. So the Chamber will then mainly concentrate on the 184 still pending, not belonging to the Kvocka and not belonging to the 500 adjudicated facts that have already been admitted. And then at a later stage, the OTP, of course, will have an opportunity to file, and then of course in due course, a list of items, if they wish to do so, from the Kvocka appeals decisions, whether or not we should put a limit to the number of those facts is still to be considered, but that might be the case. Is there -- is this a clear explanation of what the Chamber expects the parties to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's perfectly clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the next witness is subpoenaed for tomorrow, and therefore, I don't think -- I take it that he is not -- that we are not -- no. I'm making a mistake. The next witness is expected to appear tomorrow in the afternoon, upon the agreement of the parties, and we'll hear his testimony for the remainder of this week, if needed, until next Friday, and always in the afternoon. The parties have been informed about that there's a fair chance that the Chamber would not sit next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I guess I would say we're almost counting on that at this point, because the witness we had intended to subpoena has been cancelled and we don't have a substitute at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to avoid whatever is that witnesses are travelling up and down without a proper reason. Then we adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow morning, quarter -- yes, I wanted to say a quarter past 2.00, but that's in the afternoon. A quarter past 2.00 tomorrow in the afternoon.
